title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: a goddess dancing after battle who can't stop, and a god who lies down in her path
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kali, leaping from the brow of Durga's battle-form, and the poet and the priest who still called her Ma. Did you take a second look at something you'd kept your distance from? Day one thousand seventy-four.

The battle is over. The demons are gone. And Kali is still dancing. In the story people tell, she can't come down from it. Her feet pound the ground, and the ground starts to crack. The worlds shake. The gods, who were cheering a moment ago, now look at one another in alarm. Who is going to stop her? Nobody wants to walk up to Kali mid-dance and tap her on the shoulder. Then one of them has an idea, and it isn't a fight. It's an odd move, and it's the scene behind images of Kali standing on someone.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `KALI IS STILL DANCING.` → `THE WORLDS START TO SHAKE.`

segments.voice: The gods go to Shiva. Shiva doesn't pick up a weapon, and he doesn't argue with her. He walks out onto the battlefield and lies down among the fallen, right in her path. Kali, dancing blind, steps on him. And she looks down, and sees who it is. Her own husband, under her foot. In one Bengali telling, that's the moment her tongue comes out, the way someone might bite their tongue in shock: oh, no, what have I done. And the dance stops. Notice what this story is not. It isn't in the Devi Mahatmya; it's one of the stories that grew up around Kali afterward, and it's told in more than one way. Some tellings say Shiva lay down to calm her. Some say he did it so she'd recognize him. The point isn't that he beat her. Nobody beats Kali. The point is that he stopped her by being still, and by being someone she loves. Some devotees and teachers read the picture more deeply. Shiva lying there, motionless and pale, is stillness. Kali, dark and moving, is power, energy, everything that happens. The image puts them together on purpose: the dance needs the ground, and the ground, on its own, doesn't dance. Others simply love it as a family story: a wife so caught up she didn't see her husband, and the look on her face when she did. Either way, the character comes through. Kali's fierceness is real. And it stops for love.
screen: `SHIVA LIES DOWN IN HER PATH.` · `SHE STEPS ON HIM, AND SEES HIM.` · `A STORY TOLD MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `STOPPED BY STILLNESS, AND BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: lie down in the path, a little. Sit, or lie down if you can. Let your body be completely still, the way Shiva was. Notice everything that's still moving: the breath, the heartbeat, thoughts racing past, sounds outside. Don't stop any of it. Just be the still ground it all moves over. If one thought keeps dancing, let it dance, and stay still underneath it. If you pray, you can rest in the Goddess's presence. If you don't, rest in the stillness. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name over this stretch of five characters, and today, the goddess whose fierce form, as Kali, dances until stillness stops her. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, when something around you is spinning, try being the still one before you say anything. Tomorrow, Lakshmi. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: In Bengal and elsewhere, images of Kali standing on Shiva, her tongue out, are found in temples and homes, and devotees read the scene both as a family story and as a picture of stillness and power together.

fork.setup: you're one of the gods. the demons are gone, but Kali is still dancing, and the worlds are cracking. what works?

wait for her to get tired
fork.reveal: in the story, Shiva lies down among the fallen. Kali steps on him, sees her husband, and the dance stops.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kali is trampling Shiva in triumph.
what it means: in the story she steps on him mid-dance, sees him, and stops, her tongue out in shock.
what a scholar hears: the scene is not in the Devi Mahatmya; it belongs to later, especially Bengali, Kali traditions, where it is also read as Shakti moving over still Shiva.

notes: The Kali-on-Shiva story is presented as 'the story people tell', not as text. Tellings differ (Shiva lies down to calm her; to be recognized; she stops in shame or recognition). Confirm the retelling is fair and that the 'tongue out in shock' reading is attributed only to how it is 'often told in Bengal'.

The stillness/power reading (Shiva as consciousness, Kali as power) is attributed to 'some devotees and teachers'. Tomorrow's index on 1081 (Shakti as a philosophy) will develop it; here it is only touched.
